body_markdown:
This glossary defines 22 essential terms in payroll and income tax withholding, organized into five sections: Foundational Concepts, Tax Types, Employer Obligations, IRS Forms and Reporting, and Failure Modes. It serves as the vocabulary reference for distinguishing FICA, FUTA, and federal income tax withholding, the three most-conflated obligations in compliant payroll setup and filing for growth-stage companies. Most payroll compliance problems trace back to the same root cause: someone treats a payroll tax and an income tax withholding obligation as interchangeable when they are legally and structurally separate, each with its own rate, its own wage base rules, and its own filing form. Getting the underlying vocabulary right, before troubleshooting a specific paycheck or a specific filing deadline, is what makes the rest of payroll compliance tractable.


## Foundational Concepts


### Payroll Tax


Payroll tax is a mandatory employer and/or employee levy calculated as a percentage of wages paid, used to fund specific federal programs. It includes FICA (Social Security and Medicare) and FUTA, and is structurally distinct from income tax withholding. The employer FICA match alone runs 7.65% of gross wages per employee, per[IRS Publication 15](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p15.pdf) , a real cost the employer carries on top of the wages themselves. That distinction, an employer cost layered on top of wages versus a deduction taken from the employee's own pay, is the cleanest way to sort any given line item into the payroll tax bucket or the income tax withholding bucket. AsureCentral and AsureWorks both handle the payroll-tax side of a payroll run, employer match calculation and remittance, alongside the separate employee-side withholding setup described in the next entry, so the two obligations get tracked accurately within the same pay cycle instead of surfacing as a reconciliation problem at quarter-end.


### Income Tax Withholding


Income tax withholding is the portion of an employee's gross pay that an employer remits to the IRS and state agencies as an advance payment toward the employee's personal income tax liability. It carries no employer-match obligation, which is the single clearest test for telling it apart from a payroll tax: if the employer isn't also paying a matching amount out of its own pocket, the line item is income tax withholding. The amount itself is calculated from the employee's Form W-4 elections run against the IRS's current withholding tables in[Publication 15-T](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p15t.pdf) , which the IRS updates annually, so a withholding calculation that was accurate last year can turn wrong this year purely because the tables changed and nobody revisited the employee's W-4 in the meantime. A new employee's very first paycheck depends entirely on how completely they filled out that W-4; a blank or incomplete form defaults to a flat higher withholding rate under current IRS guidance, which is one of the more common sources of a first-paycheck surprise.


### Gross Wages


Gross wages are the total compensation earned by an employee before any deductions, including both payroll taxes and income tax withholding. Payroll tax rates and income tax withholding calculations are both applied to gross wages as the common starting point, which is exactly why the two obligations get confused in the first place, since they begin from the same number on the same paycheck before splitting into two entirely separate calculations. Gross wages are not the same figure for every tax purpose, however, and pre-tax deductions don't all treat the two bases the same way. A traditional 401(k) deferral reduces the income tax withholding base only, leaving the FICA base untouched, per[IRS Publication 15](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p15.pdf) . A Section 125 cafeteria plan election, including most HSA elections made through one, typically reduces both the income tax withholding base and the FICA base simultaneously, since Section 125 elections are treated differently from a standalone 401(k) deferral. A $75,000 salary with a 5% 401(k) contribution, for example, produces an income tax withholding base of $71,250 while the FICA base stays at the full $75,000, two different numbers derived from one paycheck. The same $75,000 salary with an equivalent $3,750 Section 125 HSA election instead reduces both bases together, to $71,250 for income tax withholding and $71,250 for FICA as well, since a Section 125 election doesn't carve out FICA the way a 401(k) deferral does.


### Taxable Wages


Taxable wages are the portion of gross wages subject to a specific tax. FICA taxable wages differ from federal income tax taxable wages because pre-tax deductions, such as 401(k) contributions, reduce the income tax base without touching the Social Security and Medicare base at all. The Social Security portion of FICA also caps out at an annual wage base, $184,500 for 2026, up from $176,100 in 2025, per the[Social Security Administration's contribution and benefit base table](https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html) , while Medicare has no cap whatsoever. That combination, a capped Social Security base, an uncapped Medicare base, and a pre-tax-deduction carve-out that applies to income tax withholding but not FICA, means three different numbers can describe the same paycheck depending on which tax is asking the question. Getting this wrong in either direction has a cost: capping FICA withholding too early leaves an underpayment that surfaces at year-end reconciliation, while failing to apply a pre-tax deduction correctly overstates the income tax withholding base and overwithholds the employee all year.


### Net Pay


Net pay is the amount an employee receives after all payroll tax withholdings and income tax withholdings are deducted from gross wages. It is the figure that appears as the deposit amount on a paycheck or direct deposit, and it is the only one of these terms an employee typically checks without needing to understand the mechanics behind it. The full calculation runs gross wages minus the employee's FICA share, minus federal and state income tax withholding, minus any voluntary deductions such as benefits premiums or retirement contributions. The sequence those deductions apply in can change the final result whenever pre-tax benefits are involved, since a pre-tax deduction lowers the income tax withholding base before that portion of the calculation runs, while leaving the FICA base untouched.


## Tax Types


### FICA Tax


FICA tax is the combined Federal Insurance Contributions Act levy covering Social Security (6.2%) and Medicare (1.45%) taxes, totaling 7.65% of gross wages. Both the employee and employer pay equal shares, making FICA a split-obligation payroll tax with a structure income tax withholding never has: the same 7.65% comes out of the employee's paycheck and gets matched, dollar for dollar, out of the employer's own funds. The full employer cost is 7.65% of gross wages per employee on top of the wages themselves, per[IRS Publication 15](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p15.pdf) , which is the single line item most new employers underestimate when budgeting total payroll cost, since it's easy to plan around gross wages and forget the matching share sitting on top of them. AsureCentral and AsureWorks both calculate and remit the employee and employer FICA shares as a standard part of every payroll run, whether an employer runs payroll in-house on AsureCentral or has Asure specialists manage it through AsureWorks.


### Social Security Tax


Social Security tax is the 6.2% FICA component withheld from employee wages and matched by the employer, funding the federal Social Security retirement and disability program. It applies only up to the annual wage base, $184,500 for 2026, and stops once an employee crosses that threshold for the remainder of the calendar year. The combined employee and employer rate is 12.4% up to that wage base, per the[Social Security Administration](https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html) , and the base itself rises most years, sometimes by several thousand dollars, so a payroll system that hard-codes the prior year's figure will under-withhold or over-withhold as soon as a new year starts. An employee who changes jobs mid-year adds a further wrinkle: each employer applies the wage base independently to its own payroll, so an employee who crosses the threshold at one employer and then starts a new job can end up with more Social Security tax withheld across both employers combined than the annual maximum, a mismatch the employee has to reconcile as a credit on their own personal tax return, since it spans two separate employers' payroll systems and neither one has visibility into what the other withheld.


### Medicare Tax


Medicare tax is the 1.45% FICA component withheld from all employee wages with no wage base cap, matched dollar-for-dollar by the employer. High earners pay an additional 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax on wages above $200,000 in a calendar year, and this surtax has no employer match at all. That $200,000 trigger is based purely on the individual employee's own wages for that specific employer, per[IRS guidance on the Additional Medicare Tax](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/questions-and-answers-for-the-additional-medicare-tax) ; household income and tax filing status play no role in the employer's withholding decision, which means the threshold has to be tracked employee by employee across a payroll run, individually, since there's no way to apply it as a single uniform rule across the whole payroll. An employee's eventual personal tax liability may look different once a spouse's income and joint filing status are factored in on the couple's own Form 8959, but that reconciliation happens on the employee's personal return; the employer's withholding obligation is always the flat $200,000-per-employer trigger, with no visibility into or responsibility for the employee's household tax picture.


### FUTA Tax


FUTA tax, the Federal Unemployment Tax Act tax, is an employer-only payroll tax of 6.0% on the first $7,000 of each employee's annual wages, reduced to an effective 0.6% for employers in states with no outstanding federal unemployment loans. It is never deducted from employee paychecks; the full cost sits with the employer alone. At the full 5.4% standard credit, the effective cost works out to $42 per employee per year, per the[IRS's Form 940 instructions](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i940) , a figure that hasn't moved because the $7,000 wage base itself hasn't changed since 1983, even as actual wages have grown many times over in the decades since. AsureWorks monitors each client's state unemployment loan status as part of ongoing compliance administration, since a state with an unresolved federal loan balance loses part of that credit for every employer paying FUTA in that state, raising the effective rate above 0.6% until the loan is repaid, typically in increments of roughly 0.3% for each year the loan goes unresolved.


### Federal Income Tax Withholding


Federal income tax withholding is the IRS-mandated advance collection of an employee's estimated federal income tax liability, deducted from each paycheck based on the employee's Form W-4 elections and the IRS's withholding tables. It is an employee-only obligation with no employer match, and unlike FICA and FUTA it funds the general federal budget instead of a single named program. The calculation runs off[IRS Publication 15-T](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p15t.pdf) , which the IRS revises annually, so the same W-4 elections can produce a different withholding amount from one year to the next purely because the underlying tables changed and nothing about the employee's own situation did.


### State Income Tax Withholding


State income tax withholding is the employer-remitted advance payment toward an employee's state income tax liability, calculated using state-specific withholding tables and the employee's state withholding certificate. Nine states, Alaska, Florida, Nevada, New Hampshire, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Washington, and Wyoming, levy no state income tax on wages as of 2026, which means the remaining 41 states each set their own rates, brackets, and certificate requirements. A multi-state employer has to track which of those 41 sets of rules applies to each employee's work location, and in some cases the employee's state of residence as well, since the two aren't always the same state; an employee who lives in one state and commutes across a border to work in another can trigger withholding obligations in both, depending on whether the two states have a reciprocity agreement in place.


### SUTA, State Unemployment Tax


SUTA, the State Unemployment Tax Act tax, is the state-level employer-paid unemployment insurance tax, analogous to FUTA at the federal level. Rates vary by state and by employer experience rating. SUTA payments in good standing are what generate the federal FUTA credit that reduces the gross FUTA rate from 6.0% down to the standard 0.6% effective rate. SUTA rates themselves can range from close to zero up into double digits depending on the state and the employer's own claims history, a meaningfully wider range than the flat federal FUTA rate, which is the reason two employers in different states, or with different layoff histories in the same state, can see very different total unemployment tax costs for otherwise identical payrolls. A new employer typically starts at a state's standard new-employer SUTA rate and moves onto its own experience-rated schedule after a few years, so the rate that applies in year one is rarely the rate that applies once the business has a claims history of its own. A company operating in several states carries a separate SUTA rate and a separate claims history in each one, which means a single payroll run can involve as many distinct SUTA rates as there are states with active employees, each one moving independently as claims history in that state changes.


## Employer Obligations


### Employer Tax Match


Employer tax match is the employer's obligation to contribute an amount equal to the employee's FICA withholding, 6.2% for Social Security and 1.45% for Medicare, on top of wages paid. This match is an employer expense, separate from any deduction taken out of the employee's own pay, and it is a defining feature separating payroll taxes from income tax withholding, which carries no employer match at all. The match costs 7.65% of gross wages per employee in addition to the wages themselves, which is worth budgeting for explicitly, since it means the true cost of employing someone at a given salary always runs above the salary figure itself; a $60,000 salary carries roughly $4,590 in employer FICA match on top, before FUTA, SUTA, benefits, or any other employment cost is added in. That gap between stated salary and true employer cost is one of the more common budgeting mistakes at growth-stage companies scaling headcount quickly, since a hiring plan built purely off salary figures will consistently understate actual payroll spend. AsureWorks calculates, funds, and remits the employer tax match alongside employee withholdings in each pay cycle as part of its managed payroll service, a PEO alternative with no co-employment where the client remains the employer of record, so the match is handled without the client's own team having to track it separately each cycle.


### Payroll Tax Deposit Schedule


A payroll tax deposit schedule is the IRS-assigned timetable, monthly or semi-weekly, that determines when an employer must remit withheld employee taxes and employer FICA to the IRS. The schedule is based on the employer's total payroll tax liability during a four-quarter lookback period. Employers with $50,000 or less in payroll taxes during that lookback period deposit monthly; above that threshold moves the employer to semi-weekly deposits, per[IRS Notice 931](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/n931.pdf) . A growing company can cross that $50,000 threshold mid-year as headcount or payroll expands, which shifts its deposit schedule without any separate notice arriving from the IRS to flag the change. AsureWorks tracks each client's deposit-schedule classification and reviews it against current payroll volume, so a schedule change gets caught and applied correctly before it has a chance to surface as a late deposit at the next filing.


### Trust Fund Recovery Penalty


The Trust Fund Recovery Penalty is an IRS penalty equal to 100% of unpaid trust fund taxes, the employee-withheld portions of FICA and federal income tax, assessed personally against any responsible person who willfully fails to collect or remit those taxes. It is one of the more severe payroll compliance risks a growth-stage company's officers can face. The penalty is assessed personally under[IRC Section 6672](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/employment-taxes-and-the-trust-fund-recovery-penalty-tfrp) , meaning it can attach directly to a founder, a CFO, or any officer with payroll authority, regardless of the company's own corporate liability protections; incorporating a business does not shield an individual officer from this specific penalty the way it shields them from most other business debts. AsureWorks's compliance monitoring is built to flag a deposit shortfall early, since the Trust Fund Recovery Penalty only reaches this level of exposure once a shortfall has gone unresolved long enough to look willful rather than accidental.


### Employer Identification Number


An Employer Identification Number, or EIN, is the nine-digit IRS-assigned tax ID required to file payroll tax returns, make federal tax deposits, and issue W-2s. It is the foundational credential for all payroll tax compliance and has to be obtained before the first payroll is run. The application itself is[IRS Form SS-4](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-ss-4) , and the online application returns an EIN immediately, which makes this one of the few steps in payroll setup that carries no processing-time risk, provided it's handled well before the first pay date instead of scrambled together the week payroll is due to run.


## IRS Forms and Reporting


### Form 941, Employer's Quarterly Federal Tax Return


Form 941 is the IRS quarterly return on which employers report total wages paid, employee federal income tax withheld, and both the employee and employer shares of FICA taxes. It is the primary reporting vehicle for FICA and federal income tax withholding; FUTA uses its own separate annual form instead, described next. Form 941 is filed quarterly, with due dates of April 30, July 31, October 31, and January 31, per the[IRS's Form 941 instructions](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i941) , and it is the form where the deposit-schedule classification described above gets reconciled against what was actually deposited during the quarter, so a shortfall surfaces the moment the return is filed instead of sitting undetected until a separate IRS review turns it up.


### Form 940, Employer's Annual Federal Unemployment Tax Return


Form 940 is the IRS annual return on which employers report and reconcile their FUTA tax liability for the calendar year. It covers only federal unemployment tax, standing apart from both FICA and income tax withholding, and is filed once per year, generally due January 31 of the following year. FUTA deposits themselves may be required on a quarterly basis, separate from the once-a-year filing deadline, whenever an employer's cumulative FUTA liability exceeds $500 in a quarter, per the[IRS's Form 940 instructions](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i940) ; an employer whose liability stays under that $500 mark all year simply pays the full amount when the annual return is filed.


### Form W-2, Wage and Tax Statement


Form W-2 is the annual IRS and Social Security Administration statement employers issue to each employee, reporting total wages paid and all taxes withheld, including federal income tax in Box 2, Social Security tax in Box 4, and Medicare tax in Box 6. The W-2 is a wage-and-withholding summary employees use to file their own personal income tax returns; it reports the finished results of both the payroll tax and income tax withholding calculations, without functioning as a payroll tax filing of its own. W-2s must be furnished to employees and filed with the Social Security Administration by January 31, per the[Social Security Administration's employer W-2 filing guidance](https://www.ssa.gov/employer/filingDeadlines.htm) , the same due date whether filed on paper or electronically, with no extension available on the employee-copy deadline the way there sometimes is for other information returns. AsureCentral and AsureWorks both generate and file W-2s for their respective clients, including electronic delivery to employees and electronic filing with the Social Security Administration.


## Failure Modes


### Miswithholding


Miswithholding is the error of withholding the wrong amount of federal or state income tax from an employee's paycheck, typically caused by an outdated or incorrectly completed Form W-4, a payroll system misconfiguration, or misclassifying a taxable benefit as tax-exempt. It results in an inaccurate paystub and a tax shortfall or overpayment for the employee at filing time. Miswithholding does not create direct employer tax liability on its own, since the shortfall or overpayment ultimately belongs to the employee at filing, but it still creates real employee-relations friction and compliance risk for the employer who has to explain it, and a pattern of it repeating across many employees usually points to one underlying payroll-system configuration problem, more often than it points to a string of unrelated one-off errors. AsureCentral's built-in payroll review is designed to flag W-4 mismatches and withholding anomalies before they compound across multiple pay periods, surfacing a miswithholding pattern closer to when it starts rather than months in, though the underlying W-4 or configuration issue still has to be corrected by the employer once it's flagged.


### Underwithholding


Underwithholding occurs when an employee's federal or state income tax withholding is set too low across the year, resulting in a tax balance due when the employee files their personal return. It is distinct from an employer's own underpayment of payroll taxes such as FICA or FUTA, which is an employer liability entirely separate from anything on the employee's side; underwithholding is specifically an employee-side shortfall with no direct employer penalty attached to it. The IRS applies its own underpayment penalty to employees who owe more than $1,000 at filing and didn't meet the applicable safe-harbor thresholds, tracked on[IRS Form 2210](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-2210) . An employee who takes on a large bonus, a second job, or a major life change like marriage without updating their W-4 accordingly is a common path into underwithholding, and while the penalty itself lands on the employee at filing, it's frequently the employee who comes back to payroll or HR afterward asking why the withholding didn't cover what they ended up owing.


### Deposit Shortfall


A deposit shortfall is the difference between the payroll tax amount an employer was required to deposit under its IRS-assigned deposit schedule and the amount actually deposited on time. Shortfalls on FICA and withheld income tax trigger a failure-to-deposit penalty that scales with how late the correction comes: 2% for deposits 1 to 5 days late, 5% for 6 to 15 days late, 10% for 16 or more days late, and 15% once 10 days have passed after the IRS issues a notice demanding payment, per[IRS Publication 15](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p15.pdf) . Those percentages apply to the shortfall amount itself, not the full deposit, but on a payroll of any real size even a few days' delay on a single deposit can produce a meaningful penalty, and a shortfall that recurs across multiple pay periods is exactly the kind of pattern that can eventually escalate toward Trust Fund Recovery Penalty exposure for a responsible officer. AsureWorks's payroll tax remittance is built around each client's correct deposit schedule specifically to reduce the risk of a shortfall like this, since the penalty tiers above apply automatically once a deposit misses its window, with no discretion involved on the IRS's side once that window has closed.


## How These Terms Relate


Payroll taxes and income tax withholding share the same paycheck and the same IRS remittance deadlines, but they are legally and structurally different obligations. FICA, Social Security plus Medicare, and FUTA are payroll taxes: employer-matched or employer-only levies that fund specific federal programs, each with its own rate structure and its own wage base rules. Federal and state income tax withholding are advance collections of the employee's own personal tax liability, with no employer match and no program funding behind them, just a timing mechanism that moves money to the IRS and state agencies before the employee ever files a personal return. Both categories flow through Form 941 for quarterly reporting, but FUTA stands alone on its own annual Form 940, filed on a completely different schedule. The W-2 consolidates both categories into one annual statement at year-end, which is exactly why the two get conflated in the first place: an employee looking at a single form sees federal income tax, Social Security tax, and Medicare tax all listed together, with nothing on the form itself explaining which bucket each one belongs to. Losing track of that distinction produces this hub's three named failure modes: miswithholding (the wrong income tax amount on a given paycheck), underwithholding (too little income tax withheld across the full year), and deposit shortfall (a late or short FICA or income tax remittance to the IRS), each carrying a different liability consequence and a different party who ultimately bears it. The Employer Tax Match and Trust Fund Recovery Penalty entries above sit on the payroll tax side of that same divide: both describe employer-level obligations and employer-level exposure, distinct from the employee-level consequences that miswithholding and underwithholding produce on the income tax withholding side.


## Learn More


This vocabulary covers every layer of the payroll tax versus income tax distinction, from FICA calculation and FUTA credit monitoring to W-2 filing and deposit schedule management. Growth-stage companies running payroll for the first time, or auditing an existing setup, benefit most from separating the payroll tax bucket, FICA and FUTA, from the income tax withholding bucket, federal and state, before troubleshooting any single paycheck discrepancy; most miswithholding and underwithholding questions turn out to be income tax withholding issues, while most deposit and Trust Fund Recovery Penalty exposure sits on the payroll tax side. Whether a company runs payroll in-house on AsureCentral or has Asure specialists manage it through AsureWorks, the underlying obligations described in this glossary apply the same way regardless of which model handles the day-to-day execution, and getting the vocabulary right is the first real step toward getting the calculations right. A company evaluating whether to keep payroll in-house or move it to a managed service is really deciding who applies this vocabulary correctly on its behalf; the FICA rate, the wage bases, the deposit schedule rules, and the form-to-tax mapping in this glossary hold regardless of who is running the calculations day to day.
